name: School House
narrative: Completed in 1929 and inaugurated in 1930, the School House is the oldest surviving boarding-school building in Hong Kong and a declared monument. Its H-shaped design combines Western classical columns and arches with a Chinese-style roof suited to Hong Kong's climate. It now accommodates dormitories, classrooms, staff rooms, music rooms, and the College Library.

name: Martin Hostel
narrative: Built in 1929, Martin Hostel was later named in honour of Rev. Canon E. W. L. Martin, Principal and Warden from 1928 to 1953. This Grade II historic building retains much of its original timber flooring and blends European arches and granite columns with a Chinese-style roof. It continues to serve as a student hostel and includes dining, staff, and laundry facilities.

name: Old Laboratory
narrative: The Old Laboratory was built in 1930 as part of the College's early Stanley campus and is a Grade II historic building. During the Japanese occupation, school buildings such as laboratories were adapted to house internees in the Stanley Internment Camp. Today, the building is used as staff quarters.

name: Bungalow No. 1
narrative: Bungalow No. 1 was completed in 1931 as one of the College's original staff residences. Like the other early bungalows, it forms part of the historic residential landscape of the Stanley campus and is listed as a Grade II historic building. It continues to be used as staff quarters.

name: Bungalow No. 2
narrative: Built in 1931, Bungalow No. 2 was originally a staff residence within the College's early campus plan. The single-storey bungalow is part of a group of Grade II historic buildings that recall the College's pre-war boarding-school environment. It is now used as the Principal's residence.

name: Bungalow No. 3 - Heritage Gallery
narrative: Bungalow No. 3 was constructed in 1931 as staff quarters and has retained much of its original cottage-like character. After restoration supported by heritage funding, it was converted into the Heritage Gallery in 2011. The Grade II historic building now displays artefacts and stories about the College, the Battle of Hong Kong, and the Stanley Internment Camp.

name: Bungalow No. 4 - Heritage Learning Annex
narrative: Constructed in 1931, Bungalow No. 4 is one of the College's historic staff residences and is a Grade II historic building. Together with Bungalow No. 3, it was restored to support the College's heritage education programme. It now serves as the Heritage Learning Annex, providing space for heritage learning and related activities.

name: Bungalow No. 5
narrative: Bungalow No. 5 was built in 1931 as a staff residence and is part of the College's Grade II historic bungalow group. During the final months of the Japanese occupation, it was accidentally bombed in an American air raid on 16 January 1945, causing civilian casualties among internees. It is now used as staff quarters.

name: St. Stephen's Chapel
narrative: Opened in 1950 at the highest point of the campus, St. Stephen's Chapel is a Grade III historic building. It was built as a memorial to people who suffered and died during the Second World War and the Japanese occupation, including victims associated with the Stanley Internment Camp. The Chapel remains a place for worship, prayer, school services, and remembrance.

name: Ng Wah Hall
narrative: Ng Wah Hall was completed in 1970, during a period when St. Stephen's College was expanding after becoming co-educational. It provides a dedicated indoor venue for assemblies, performances, ceremonies, and other large school events. The hall is also listed as a Grade III historic building.

name: Classroom Block
narrative: The Classroom Block was built in 1964 to provide additional teaching space for the growing College. It reflects the post-war development of the campus and is listed as a Grade III historic building. It continues to house classrooms for daily teaching and learning.

name: North House
narrative: North House was completed in 1952 as part of the College's post-war rebuilding and recovery. It helped restore and expand the College's residential capacity after the wartime damage to the campus. Today, it remains a student dormitory.

name: Tang Shiu Kin Sports Field
narrative: The Tang Shiu Kin Sports Field began as a swamp that was filled in during the 1920s to reduce the risk of malaria. During the Japanese occupation, it became a vegetable garden connected with the Stanley Internment Camp, and it was renamed after Sir Tang Shiu Kin funded its re-turfing in 1975. Following later refurbishments, it now provides a football pitch, athletics facilities, and space for physical education.

name: Benevolence House
narrative: Benevolence House was inaugurated in 2022 as a major contemporary addition to the campus. Its design connects the historic school buildings with the sports field, while its sea-facing side contains classrooms and the Carol Yang Black Box Theatre. It now provides classrooms, a grand hall, an indoor fitness centre, student facilities, and an outdoor auditorium.

name: Special Room Block
narrative: The Special Room Block was opened in 1980 on the site of a former tennis court, replacing the old laboratory as the College expanded its specialist facilities. Designed by Dr. Tao Ho, its distinctive sloping walls and corridor layout earned a Hong Kong Institute of Architects Merit Award in 1982. The building now contains classrooms, science laboratories, computer rooms, and specialised teaching spaces.

name: Wilson Wang Water Sports Centre
narrative: The Wilson Wang Water Sports Centre was completed in 1982 to strengthen the College's sporting facilities. Its establishment reflects the College's long-standing emphasis on residential education, physical development, and use of its coastal Stanley setting. It is now used as the College's swimming centre.

name: Alex Y. D. Au Building
narrative: The Alex Y. D. Au Building was completed in 1982 as part of the College's continuing campus expansion. It centralised dining facilities for students and staff in a building named in recognition of its benefactor. It is now home to the school dining hall and tuck shop.

name: Luke Yip Building
narrative: Completed in 1985 as the Administration Building, this building was later renamed the Luke Yip Building. It was developed to support the College's expanding administrative and teaching needs. It now contains the school office and staff rooms.

name: Leung Kau Kui Student Centre
narrative: The Leung Kau Kui Student Centre was completed in 1988 to provide additional student-focused learning space. Its construction reflects the College's effort to broaden facilities beyond the original historic core of the campus. It is now used for classrooms and student activities.

name: Centenary Building
narrative: The Centenary Building was opened in 2006 to commemorate the 100th anniversary of St. Stephen's College, which was founded in 1903. It was designed to provide interactive learning facilities, including a language laboratory and student activity spaces, and was expanded in 2010 as classroom demand increased. Today, it provides classrooms and features a green facade with rooftop solar panels.

name: College House
narrative: College House was completed in 2011-12 as a modern two-wing residence for boarders. It expanded the College's long tradition of boarding education, which has been central to school life since its founding. It continues to provide dormitory accommodation for students.
